cards.front: A survival-factor withdrawal experiment finds that blocking RNA or protein synthesis delays neuronal death. Why does this support an active death program?
cards.back: Death requires new gene expression. Blocking synthesis delays the process, indicating that the neuron actively produces components needed to die.
cards.quote: Instead the neuron has to make something in order to die.

cards.front: How do the cell shape and membrane changes of apoptosis differ from those of necrosis?
cards.back: Apoptosis shrinks the cell and packages it into membrane-wrapped fragments. Necrosis swells the cell, disrupts membranes and spills contents, inflaming surrounding tissue.
cards.quote: the cell shrinks, its chromatin condenses into dense clumps, and it breaks into membrane-wrapped pieces that other cells swallow.

cards.front: A densely condensed nucleus seen during apoptosis is called {{c1::pyknotic}}.
cards.quote: A nucleus condensed this way is called pyknotic, and pyknotic nuclei were what researchers counted in early studies of neuron death in embryos.

cards.front: After tissue trauma, cells swell and their membranes rupture. What local tissue response is expected, and why?
cards.back: Inflammation is expected: this necrotic pattern releases cellular contents into the surrounding tissue.
cards.quote: the cell swells, its membranes fail and its contents spill out, inflaming the tissue around it.

cards.front: Which two C. elegans genes are required for the core programmed cell-death pathway?
cards.back: ced-3 and ced-4. Strong loss-of-function mutants retain cells that normally die; some surviving cells develop neuronal features.
cards.quote: two genes, ced-3 and ced-4, that are needed for programmed cell death.

cards.front: Why is CED-9 considered a brake on cell death in C. elegans?
cards.back: Gain of CED-9 function preserves doomed cells; loss kills cells that normally survive. Thus its normal role is protective.
cards.quote: a gain-of-function mutation kept doomed cells alive, and loss of ced-9 killed cells that should have lived.

cards.front: In a death pathway, loss of inhibitor R causes extra deaths; deleting protease K as well suppresses them. What genetic relationship follows, and does this prove direct binding?
cards.back: R restrains a death pathway requiring K and acts upstream in genetic order. Suppression alone does not show that the proteins touch.
cards.quote: if removing the killer cancels the effect of removing the brake, the brake works through the killer.

cards.front: In the core C. elegans death pathway, {{c1::EGL-1}} binds CED-9 to release the protective brake.
cards.back: Its resemblance to the BCL-2 family is confined to a BH3 domain.
cards.quote: it binds CED-9 to release the brake, and is needed for most somatic cell deaths in the worm.

cards.front: Caspases use an active-site cysteine to cleave targets just after {{c1::aspartate}}.
cards.quote: Caspases cut with a cysteine in their active site, just after an aspartate in their target.

cards.front: How does activation of initiator caspases lead to cellular dismantling?
cards.back: Inactive initiator precursors activate when gathered onto a platform. They cut and activate executioner caspases, which cleave many cellular proteins.
cards.quote: Initiator caspases switch on when they are gathered onto a platform, and they then cut and activate executioner caspases,

cards.front: Which mammalian proteins correspond to the worm death proteins CED-3 and CED-4?
cards.back: CED-3 corresponds to caspases; CED-4 corresponds to Apaf-1, which gathers and activates initiator caspases.
cards.quote: CED-4 later proved related to mammalian Apaf-1,

cards.front: How do worm CED-9 and mammalian Bcl-2 differ in where they restrain the death pathway?
cards.back: CED-9 directly holds back CED-4. Mammalian Bcl-2 family protectors instead guard mitochondrial cytochrome c release.
cards.quote: Bcl-2 belongs to the BCL-2 family, whose members decide whether mitochondria release cytochrome c;

cards.front: Why should mammalian Apaf-1 dependence on cytochrome c not be assumed for worm CED-4?
cards.back: The counterparts differ: Apaf-1 needs cytochrome c, whereas cytochrome c has no clear role in worm apoptosis.
cards.quote: once bound to cytochrome c, Apaf-1 gathers and switches on initiator caspases

cards.front: Target-derived NGF signals through the receptor {{c1::TrkA}} on sympathetic neuron axon terminals.
cards.quote: NGF made by the target acts through its receptor TrkA on the neuron's axon terminals
cards.section: The first brake: from a lost signal to cytochrome c

cards.front: How does loss of NGF promote Bim gene expression in young sympathetic neurons?
cards.back: JNK activates c-Jun, promoting pro-death gene expression. Reduced Akt restraint frees FOXO factors, which are thought to help induce Bim.
cards.quote: Among the genes then induced are BH3-only proteins such as Bim; freed FOXO factors are thought to help switch Bim on.
cards.section: The first brake: from a lost signal to cytochrome c

cards.front: A young sympathetic neuron lacks Bim alone and loses NGF. Should apoptosis be abolished, and why?
cards.back: No; death is slowed rather than abolished. Other BH3-only proteins share the pro-death work, so removing Bim alone leaves alternative contributors.
cards.quote: Other BH3-only proteins share the work, and neurons lacking Bim alone die more slowly rather than not at all.
cards.section: The first brake: from a lost signal to cytochrome c

cards.front: How can Bim promote opening of the mitochondrial gate in a deprived sympathetic neuron?
cards.back: Its BH3 domain occupies protective BCL-2 protein grooves, releasing restraint on Bax. Bim can also activate Bax directly.
cards.quote: Protectors with their grooves filled can no longer hold Bax back, and Bim can also activate Bax directly.
cards.section: The first brake: from a lost signal to cytochrome c

cards.front: Before its release during apoptosis, cytochrome c normally carries {{c1::electrons}} inside mitochondria.
cards.quote: Cytochrome c, which normally carries electrons inside the mitochondrion, escapes into the cytoplasm.
cards.section: The first brake: from a lost signal to cytochrome c

cards.front: After cytochrome c binds Apaf-1 in a young sympathetic neuron, which complex and caspase sequence follow?
cards.back: The apoptosome assembles and activates initiator caspase-9, which activates executioner caspase-3.
cards.quote: Apaf-1 assembles into a wheel-shaped complex, the apoptosome, which gathers and activates the initiator caspase-9.
cards.section: The first brake: from a lost signal to cytochrome c

cards.front: Bax-null sympathetic neurons lose NGF. What happens to upstream death signaling, mitochondrial cytochrome c and cell size?
cards.back: Upstream signaling can still change: Akt activity falls and c-Jun/Bim rise. Cytochrome c stays mitochondrial, so the neurons survive, but they shrink because NGF also supports growth.
cards.quote: Steps 1 and 2 lie upstream of Bax, so they should still happen: Akt activity falls, and c-Jun and Bim rise.
cards.section: The first brake: from a lost signal to cytochrome c

cards.front: The susceptibility to injected cytochrome c acquired by NGF-deprived sympathetic neurons is called {{c1::competence-to-die}}.
cards.quote: Deshmukh called this acquired susceptibility competence-to-die. It built up gradually over roughly the first day without NGF:
cards.section: The second brake: competence to die

cards.front: Injected cytochrome c spares NGF-supported sympathetic neurons but kills day-deprived neurons whose mitochondrial gate was held shut. What extra control point is required?
cards.back: A restraint downstream of cytochrome c release. Injection bypasses the gate in both groups, yet only deprivation permits caspase-dependent death.
cards.quote: So something below cytochrome c release also changes when NGF is taken away.
cards.section: The second brake: competence to die

cards.front: NGF-deprived sympathetic neurons become sensitive to injected cytochrome c both when protein synthesis is blocked and when Bax is absent. What separates this sensitization from opening the mitochondrial gate?
cards.back: Acquiring competence needs neither new proteins nor Bax. The two-brake rule separates gene-expression-dependent gate opening from loss of the downstream caspase restraint; either treatment holds the gate shut while sensitization proceeds.
cards.quote: Neurons making no new protein became competent, and so did neurons lacking Bax.
cards.section: The second brake: competence to die

cards.front: Why can XIAP effectively restrain caspases in young NGF-dependent sympathetic neurons?
cards.back: These neurons have little Apaf-1. Few apoptosomes generate a caspase signal small enough for XIAP to block; deprivation lowers XIAP.
cards.quote: with few apoptosomes, the caspase signal is small enough to block.
cards.section: The second brake: competence to die

cards.front: Cytochrome c and Smac are injected together into young sympathetic neurons kept in NGF. What happens and why?
cards.back: They die: cytochrome c bypasses the mitochondrial gate, and Smac removes the caspase inhibition that otherwise protects NGF-supported neurons.
cards.quote: When cytochrome c was injected along with Smac, a mitochondrial protein that removes inhibitors from caspases, neurons kept in NGF died too.
cards.section: The second brake: competence to die

cards.front: A young sympathetic neuron loses NGF for about a day while protein synthesis is blocked, then receives cytoplasmic cytochrome c. What happens and why?
cards.back: It dies within hours. Blocking synthesis holds the mitochondrial gate shut but does not prevent competence; injection bypasses the remaining gate.
cards.quote: Cytochrome c killed them within hours, a control injection did not, and a caspase inhibitor prevented the death.
cards.section: The second brake: competence to die

cards.front: A cell-death model has a mitochondrial release gate and a downstream protease inhibitor. Delivering the released signal directly still spares cells. Design a test of the downstream restraint.
cards.back: Compare signal alone, inhibitor removal alone and both, with delivery controls. The two-brake rule predicts death when both barriers are bypassed; rescue by a protease inhibitor would support protease-dependent execution.
cards.quote: The neuron dies by apoptosis only when the gate is open (or skipped by injection) and the caspase brake is off.
cards.section: The second brake: competence to die

cards.front: Healthy cells normally keep phosphatidylserine on the {{c1::inner}} face of the plasma membrane.
cards.quote: A healthy cell keeps the lipid phosphatidylserine on the inner face of its plasma membrane.
cards.section: Cleaning up: the corpse sends a signal

cards.front: How does an apoptotic cell use membrane lipid rearrangement to promote its removal?
cards.back: In studied cells, caspases disrupt phosphatidylserine retention and activate a scramblase. Exposed phosphatidylserine becomes an external signal recognized by phagocytes.
cards.quote: phosphatidylserine appears outside, where receptors on phagocytes recognize it as an "eat me" signal.
cards.section: Cleaning up: the corpse sends a signal

cards.front: Which resident immune cells are the main corpse-engulfing cells in the vertebrate brain and spinal cord?
cards.back: Microglia.
cards.quote: In the vertebrate brain and spinal cord the main phagocytes are microglia, the brain's resident immune cells;
cards.section: Cleaning up: the corpse sends a signal

cards.front: Apoptotic cells expose phosphatidylserine normally, but phagocytes cannot recognize it. What happens to corpse clearance and visible corpse abundance, and why?
cards.back: Clearance should slow and visible corpses should accumulate, assuming death production is unchanged. The exposed lipid cannot recruit normal recognition and engulfment.
cards.quote: A developing brain kills many cells, yet at any moment few dead cells are visible, because they are removed quickly.
cards.section: Cleaning up: the corpse sends a signal

cards.front: A cell binds annexin V at its surface. Which apoptotic membrane change does this report, and does binding alone show membrane rupture?
cards.back: It reports exposed phosphatidylserine. It does not by itself show rupture: apoptotic cells can expose the lipid and be engulfed before their membranes fail.
cards.quote: The same exposure lets researchers label apoptotic cells with annexin V, a protein that binds phosphatidylserine.
cards.section: Cleaning up: the corpse sends a signal

cards.front: Why did loss of caspase-3 or caspase-9 fail to establish permanent survival of developing mouse spinal and peripheral neurons?
cards.back: The same number eventually died, but later and with altered, non-apoptotic morphology. Blocking the apoptotic route did not block every route to death.
cards.quote: That is the first limit of the two-brake rule: it gates the apoptotic route, not every way a neuron can die.

cards.front: Hypothetically, each of two ganglia peaks at 24,000 neurons. Later, wild type has 15,000 and a Bax-null ganglion has 21,000. With no neuron addition, what percentage of wild-type deaths was prevented?
cards.quote: naturally occurring death was largely eliminated in many neuron populations of Bax-null mice.

cards.front: In a hypothetical nerve, Bax deletion yields 50% more axons than the wild-type count. What percentage of the mutant axons are extra relative to wild type?
cards.back: Let wild type = N; mutant = 1.50N and extra = 0.50N. Extra fraction = 0.50N/1.50N × 100 ≈ 33.3%.
cards.quote: myelinated axons were about 30 to 55 percent more numerous than in normal mice

cards.front: Blocking a death pathway lets neurons survive loss of a target-derived factor, but their axons still fail to innervate targets. What additional function is implicated, and why compare with death-blocked neurons retaining the factor?
cards.back: The factor also supports target innervation. Keeping the death block in both groups separates that function from survival and controls for the block itself; this uses the rule that survival rescue exposes remaining developmental defects.
cards.quote: NGF is therefore needed for axons to grow into many targets, as well as for survival.

cards.front: In embryos and newborns, do NGF/Bax double-null mice show an equally severe sympathetic innervation defect in every organ?
cards.back: No. Relative to Bax-null mice retaining NGF, defects range from absent or nearly absent innervation in salivary glands to normal innervation in the trachea.
cards.quote: In embryos and newborns, the axons failed to fully innervate many targets, and the failure differed by organ.

cards.front: How could late, sparse Bax deletion test for a role in neurons that already survived developmental death, and what would a normal result fail to exclude?
cards.back: Delete Bax after the death period and compare deleted neurons with normal neighbours. Shrinkage or contact loss, reversed by restoring Bax, supports a later role. The timing rule means a normal result cannot exclude an earlier role.
cards.quote: If they stay normal, this test found no such job at that age; it cannot rule out an earlier one.

cards.front: Bax is deleted in scattered neurons before developmental death. If limited trophic support alone causes small size, which Bax-deleted cells should be small?
cards.back: Roughly the fraction normally destined to die should be small; the rest should resemble normal neighbours. If ordinarily surviving cells also shrink, limited support alone is insufficient.
cards.quote: If limited support alone explains the size, roughly the share that would normally have died (about half in many peripheral populations) should be small

cards.front: Neurons preserved by a death-pathway deletion remain small; supplying trophic factor restores their size. What does this rescue establish, and what broader conclusion would overreach?
cards.back: Insufficient trophic support is a sufficient explanation for the small size under these conditions. The rescue rule does not exclude other functions of the deleted gene in other populations or developmental periods.
cards.quote: if it restores size, limited support is a sufficient explanation.

cards.front: Why do enlarged forebrains in some caspase-3 or caspase-9 knockout mice not contradict continued spinal and peripheral neuron death?
cards.back: The forebrain phenotype largely reflects reduced early progenitor death, a different population and stage. Caspase-3 knockout severity also depends on genetic background.
cards.quote: This reflects reduced death early in neurogenesis, largely among progenitors, not a block of the trophic deaths this lesson follows.

cards.front: Which apoptosome component is largely silenced in fully mature neurons?
cards.back: Apaf-1.
cards.quote: In fully mature neurons Apaf-1 is largely silenced,

cards.front: XIAP is removed and cytochrome c injected into a mature neuron with very little Apaf-1. Must it die, and why?
cards.back: No. Removing the caspase brake need not suffice because little Apaf-1 may limit apoptosome assembly. The young sympathetic neuron result cannot be assumed at every age.
cards.quote: In mature neurons, with little Apaf-1, removing XIAP need not be enough.

cards.front: A caspase inhibitor preserves trophically deprived axons but fails to preserve severed axons. How should this affect claims that the sympathetic neuron two-brake rule explains all axon loss?
cards.back: It argues for distinct routes. The stated rule gates apoptosis after trophic deprivation; local trophic axon degeneration uses caspases, whereas injury-induced breakdown follows another route. Neither result establishes a universal mechanism for pruning in vivo.
cards.quote: while an axon cut by injury breaks down by a different route.
